case_info.scenario: An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

[Locution: assert — type: fact]
Assert t as a valid instance of the given type (stronger commitment).

Apply this deliberation move in your response.

    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered

In this case, the justification for its use was the observed peripheral traction with subretinal fluid during hyaloid removal, which posed a risk of retinal detachment. Its application allowed for controlled endolaser photocoagulation and subsequent air-fluid exchange to secure the retina.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.

       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Clinical case]
An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

Its application allowed for controlled endolaser photocoagulation and subsequent air-fluid exchange to secure the retina.
[Doctor]: 
[AI Assistant]: Indeed, PFO's high specific gravity and immiscibility with water make it an effective intraoperative tool to mechanically stabilize the retina, especially in pediatric eyes with complex anatomy from persistent fetal vasculature. The subsequent finding of small retained PFO bubbles outside the macula, while not ideal, did not compromise the primary surgical goal of retinal attachment.

The critical fact is that PFO's intraoperative role was specifically indicated by the direct observation of peripheral traction with subretinal fluid, a sight-threatening complication that required immediate stabilization to prevent detachment.

Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.

       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   Scoring:

An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

1. Mental Demand

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

[Clinical case]
An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

In this case, the justification for its use was the observed peripheral traction with subretinal fluid during hyaloid removal, which posed a risk of retinal detachment. Its application allowed for controlled endolaser photocoagulation and subsequent air-fluid exchange to secure the retina.
[Doctor]: 
[AI Assistant]: Indeed, PFO's high specific gravity and immiscibility with water make it an effective intraoperative tool to mechanically stabilize the retina, especially in pediatric eyes with complex anatomy from persistent fetal vasculature. Its use here was crucial to address the tractional forces and subretinal fluid identified during surgery, facilitating subsequent laser treatment and tamponade. The subsequent finding of small retained PFO bubbles outside the macula, while not ideal, did not compromise the primary surgical goal of retinal attachment.
[Doctor]: 
[AI Assistant]: You've correctly identified the key properties of PFO that justified its use. The critical fact is that PFO's intraoperative role was specifically indicated by the direct observation of peripheral traction with subretinal fluid, a sight-threatening complication that required immediate stabilization to prevent detachment.
[Doctor]: 
[AI Assistant]: Exactly, the direct visualization of traction with subretinal fluid was the immediate surgical indication for PFO, as it provided the necessary counterforce to flatten the retina and enable definitive treatment.  Can you clarify what specific intraoperative findings or principles of vitreoretinal surgery made PFO the optimal choice over, say, a direct drainage of subretinal fluid without heavy liquid?

case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

[Case]
An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.
